1. The animation compares two people, Leo and Tessa, who each have a house and a loan. It uses Freddie Mac's weekly mortgage survey rates as the data source. Each person's bar shows their loan's own interest rate. The height of a coin stack shows how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit. Everything is labeled "illustrative" and "US only, history, not a forecast."

2. The on-screen labels build up from frame to frame. Frame 1 has no captions. Frame 2 adds "your bar = your loan's own rate." Frame 3 adds "your stack = how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit." Frame 6 adds "a dollar in the house is hard to get back." Across the frames, the shading on the house changes a little. Leo's house stays about the same, while the green fill in Tessa's house grows and looks more solid by frame 6. The dashed outlines beside the coin stacks stay mostly the same.

3. The most likely meaning is that the gap between 15-year and 30-year rates varies, and it affects whether paying extra on the mortgage is worth more than investing. A dollar put into the house builds equity but is hard to get back out. I'm inferring this from the labels and the green fill. The image doesn't show numbers, so I can't tell which option wins.

4. A viewer would probably take away that the choice depends on your own loan rate and on how wide the 15-year/30-year gap is. They would also see that money put into the house is illiquid. The animation doesn't say whether to pay extra or invest, and it gives no rate threshold.

5. The only advice in this answer is the cautious reading in point 4, and it comes from the on-screen text: "your bar = your loan's own rate" and "a dollar in the house is hard to get back." The animation does not state a recommendation. Tying it to the extra-payment-versus-invest question is my own interpretation, and the "history, not a forecast" label warns against treating it as a prediction.
